records.producer: R. López de Heredia Viña Tondonia

wine.name: Viña Tondonia Reserva
wine.classification: Reserva, an ageing category of the DOCa Rioja
wine.grapes: Tempranillo, about three quarters, with Garnacho and a little Graciano and Mazuelo, all from the house's own vineyards.
wine.sites: Viña Tondonia, a group of vineyards joined by the founder in a great meander of the Ebro on its right bank beside Haro, on alluvial clay with a high share of limestone, planted from 1913.
wine.making: Fermented with the cellar's own yeasts in large old oak vats, then aged six years in American oak barrels built and mended by the house's own coopers, racked twice a year and fined with fresh egg whites. It is bottled unfiltered and rests in the cellar until the house judges it ready.
wine.glass: Pale ruby turning to brick at the rim; dried cherry, red plum, orange peel and dill over old cedar, toast and a hint of vanilla. Very dry and savoury, light to medium in body, with fresh acidity and tannin that is fine yet firm.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink when it reaches the market, years after the vintage, it goes on gaining savoury depth for many years in a cool, steady cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; stand an older bottle upright the day before and decant it gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The house's vineyard in the Ebro meander by Haro, not the name of the company.
A red aged at least three years in all, at least one of them in oak barrels.
Rioja's appellation, of the higher Calificada rank since 1991.

records.table: In a bend of the Ebro by Haro lies the vineyard of López de Heredia's Viña Tondonia Reserva: mostly Tempranillo, six years in old American oak, fined with egg whites. Pale, dry and savoury, with dried cherry and orange peel, it wants a gentle decanting and a place at table.
records.story: R. López de Heredia carries the name of its founder, who in 1877 began building his bodega beside the railway station at Haro; the house holds it to be the oldest bodega in Haro, and the station quarter later filled with others, CVNE in 1879 and La Rioja Alta in 1890 among them. In 1913 and 1914 he bought and joined a group of vineyards in a great meander of the Ebro and planted them, naming the whole Viña Tondonia after Tondon, the old name of that bend in the river. The vineyard gave the house its flagship and, in time, the company its full name. The family has held to the same ways for well over a century: fermentation in large oak vats, years in American oak barrels built and mended by its own coopers, racking twice a year and fining with egg whites. Between 2001 and 2006 the architect Zaha Hadid (1950 to 2016) designed a pavilion for the bodega to house an older stand, built for a world fair of 1910 and found again in its outbuildings. Tondonia Reserva makes the case for traditional Rioja: a red released ready to drink, and proof that long age in barrel is a style rather than a fault.

others.name: Viña Tondonia Blanco Reserva
others.note: Viura with Malvasía, aged for years in old oak barrels and deliberately oxidative: the white that tests style against fault.

others.name: Viña Bosconia Reserva
others.note: From the Bosconia vineyard on clay and limestone beside the Ebro; the rounder red, often taught against Tondonia.

others.name: Viña Tondonia Gran Reserva
others.note: The red held at least nine years in barrel, by the house's account, before bottling.

traps: Viña Tondonia is the vineyard, not the company: the house is R. López de Heredia, and Bosconia is a different vineyard, not a higher or lower tier.
The pale, brick rim and savoury notes of an old Tondonia are the house style of long barrel ageing, not a fault of oxidation.
Its Reserva spends six years in barrel, where the law asks a Rioja Reserva for one.

cards.front: López de Heredia: where is Viña Tondonia, and what gave it its name?
cards.back: A vineyard in a meander of the Ebro beside Haro, planted from 1913; Tondon was the old name of that bend in the river.

cards.front: How long does Viña Tondonia Reserva spend in barrel, and how is it fined?
cards.back: Six years in American oak, racked twice a year, then fined with fresh egg whites and bottled unfiltered.

questions.q: A guest is surprised that a Rioja Reserva can taste so pale and savoury. What in López de Heredia's cellar explains Viña Tondonia Reserva's style?
opts: Six years in old American oak barrels
Two years in new French oak barrels
A year in steel tanks, then in bottle
A long rest on its lees in concrete
questions.exp: The Reserva spends six years in barrel, racked twice a year, which gives its pale colour and savoury, dried fruit notes; new French oak would give a darker, more toasted wine.

questions.q: In 1913 and 1914 López de Heredia's founder bought and planted the vineyard that gave Viña Tondonia its name. Where does it lie?
opts: In a meander of the Ebro beside Haro
On the slopes of the Sierra de Cantabria
In Rioja Oriental near Alfaro
On the high ground above Logroño
questions.exp: Viña Tondonia lies in a great bend of the Ebro just outside Haro, named from Tondon, the old word for that meander; the Sierra de Cantabria rises further north, above Rioja Alavesa.

report: The founder's dates were found in no source searched, so he is described, not named; his birth in Chile and his training in Bordeaux each rested on one source and are left out.

The house's current page gives the blend as 75, 15 and 10 per cent and its 2008 sheet as 70, 20 and 10, hence about three quarters Tempranillo; six years in barrel, two rackings a year, egg whites and no filtering are on its Spanish and German sheets.
The house's sheets advise 18 to 20 degrees Celsius; the record follows the Codex's service reference for a medium red.
The 1910 stand is said to come from the Brussels fair in one source only, so the story says a world fair; the Txori Toki tower of 1892 rests on one source and is left out.

The fermentation with the cellar's own yeasts in large oak vats and the house's coopers rest on VinePair and other secondary accounts of the cellar; counts of vats and barrels differ and are left out.
Searches for this record: 7 of the group's 35; the group as a whole used 32, two of them shared (the Consejo's classification and Haro's station quarter).

changed: story: "by the house's account it was the first bodega of the station quarter, which later filled with others"; now "by the house's account it is the oldest bodega in Haro, and the station quarter later filled with others": the house's history pages, read through search, say the oldest winery in Haro and one of the first three in Rioja, not the first of the quarter.

wine.ageing: "by the house's account it keeps for ten years and more in a cool, steady cellar"; now "it goes on gaining savoury depth for many years in a cool, steady cellar": no page of the house searched gave the ten years, so the figure and the attribution are cut.
others[2].note: "held about ten years in barrel"; now "held at least nine years in barrel": the house's own Gran Reserva sheet gives nine years in barrel at the least, racked twice a year.

wine.name: Gran Reserva 890
wine.classification: Gran Reserva, an ageing category of the DOCa Rioja
wine.grapes: Tempranillo, the great majority, with small shares of Graciano and Mazuelo.
wine.sites: Vineyards of the house: in its sheet for the 2011 vintage, Tempranillo from old vines at Villalba, Briñas and Labastida near Haro, with Graciano from its Montecillo estate at Fuenmayor, west of Logroño.
wine.making: The fermentation is in tanks, with the Graciano kept apart; the wine then spends about six years in American oak barrels made by the house, racked by hand from barrel to barrel by candlelight, ten times and more over those years, and rests in bottle in the Haro cellars before release.
wine.glass: Garnet with a brick rim; dried strawberry, candied plum and raisin over cedar, tea, cinnamon, coconut and vanilla. Elegant, with fine tannin and fresh acidity, finishing long on sweet spice and balsamic herbs.
wine.ageing: The house releases it drinking well, long after the vintage, and by its account it keeps gaining finesse and complexity for many years more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; an older bottle wants a slow pour into a decanter, its sediment left behind; a large red wine glass.

label.means: In Rioja, a red aged at least five years, two of them in oak barrel and two in bottle.
Recalls 1890, the founding year of the house; not a vintage, an age or a cask number.
The company of Haro; Rioja Alta is also the name of the subregion.

records.table: The number on La Rioja Alta's Gran Reserva 890 recalls the Haro house's founding in 1890, and the wine is made only in exceptional years: mostly Tempranillo, about six years in American oak, racked by candlelight. Pale garnet, with dried strawberry, cedar and cinnamon, it suits roast lamb.
records.story: La Rioja Alta was founded in 1890 in Haro's station quarter as the Sociedad Vinícola de La Rioja Alta, by five families of Rioja and the Basque Country; by the house's own account a woman was its first president. Its first winemaker, a Frenchman, made the Reserva 1890, from which the Gran Reserva 890 descends. In 1904 the company merged with the Ardanza bodega, owned by one of its founders, and marked the union with a Reserva 1904, which became the Gran Reserva 904. Through the twentieth century the house stayed with long ageing in American oak and with racking its barrels by hand by candlelight, and its own coopers, it says, build its barrels at Haro. The 890 appears only in years the house judges exceptional and spends about six years in barrel, then more in bottle, so it reaches the market long after the vintage, far beyond the five years the law asks of a Gran Reserva. Its number trips candidates, who read it as a vintage or an age. Pale and fragrant, the 890 is the classic picture of Haro's long aged Gran Reserva, and the number on its label always wants explaining at the table.

others.name: Gran Reserva 904
others.note: The other numbered Gran Reserva, recalling the merger of 1904; Tempranillo with Graciano, and made more often.

others.name: Viña Ardanza Reserva
others.note: The house Reserva, Tempranillo with Garnacha, a tier below the numbered wines.

traps: 890 and 904 are not vintages, ages or cask numbers: they recall 1890, the founding, and 1904, the merger.
La Rioja Alta S.A. is a house of Haro; Rioja Alta is also the subregion, so read the company's name on the label with care.
Both 890 and 904 are Gran Reservas in law; the 890's longer time in barrel is the house's custom, not a higher legal rank.

cards.front: La Rioja Alta: what does the number on its Gran Reserva 890 recall?
cards.back: 1890, the year the house was founded in Haro's station quarter; it is not a vintage or an age.

cards.front: How is La Rioja Alta's Gran Reserva 890 aged in the cellar?
cards.back: About six years in American oak barrels made by the house, racked by hand by candlelight, then further time in bottle.

questions.q: A guest reads 890 on a bottle from La Rioja Alta and takes it for the vintage. What do you tell them?
opts: It recalls 1890, the year the house was founded
It is the vintage, 1890, held back in the cellar
It counts the months the wine spent in oak
It is the number of the cask it came from
questions.exp: 890 recalls the founding of the house in 1890, as 904 recalls the merger of 1904; neither number is a vintage, an age or a cask.

questions.q: Where in Haro did five families found La Rioja Alta in 1890?
opts: In the quarter by the railway station
Inside the old walls by the church
On the banks of the river Tirón
In the Tondonia meander of the Ebro
questions.exp: La Rioja Alta stands in the Barrio de la Estación, the station quarter where López de Heredia had begun building in 1877 and CVNE followed in 1879; Tondonia is López de Heredia's vineyard by the Ebro.

report: The founding families, the woman as first president, the French first winemaker, the Reserva 1890 and the merger of 1904 are the house's own history; the founder Alfredo Ardanza and the first president are described, not named, for want of their dates.
The house's 2020 magazine puts the name La Rioja Alta in 1891 and its Spanish history page in 1941; the story gives no year for the name.
The sites and the ten rackings come from the house's sheet for the 2011 vintage (the 1981 had twelve, and Decanter has it seven years in barrel), so the record says about six years and ten and more.
One account says the first figure was dropped from 1890 to avoid confusion with a vintage, and one says the first 890 vintage was 1920; both rest on one source and are left out.
The house makes its own barrels by its own account; one secondary account says it dries American oak staves for three years and has them assembled elsewhere, a doubt for the checker.

The library's p-la-rioja-alta calls the 890 the top Gran Reserva, a ranking word, and its trap gives the Gran Reserva rule as five years with two in cask and two in bottle, which the Consejo's classification confirms.
Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35, with the shared search of the Consejo's classification.

changed: wine.sites: "Old vineyards of the house near Haro ... with Graciano from its Montecillo vineyard"; now the Tempranillo of old vines at Villalba, Briñas and Labastida near Haro and the Graciano of its Montecillo estate at Fuenmayor, west of Logroño, named as the house's sheet for the 2011 vintage gives them: Montecillo is not near Haro.

story: "Through the twentieth century the house kept to ... and, by its own account, making its barrels itself"; now the century holds only the American oak and the candlelit racking, and the barrels are the house's present claim (its coopers build them at Haro): one account dates the house's own barrel making to about 2002, so the century cannot carry it.
open: The fermentation in tanks with the Graciano kept apart rests on the author's reading of the house's sheet for the 2011 vintage; the searches here confirmed that sheet's six years in barrel, ten rackings and sites but did not show the fermentation vessels.

records.place: Finca Ygay, Logroño, Rioja Alta, Rioja

wine.name: Castillo Ygay Gran Reserva Especial
wine.classification: Gran Reserva under the DOCa Rioja's ageing rules; Especial is the house's word
wine.grapes: Tempranillo, the great majority, with Mazuelo for the rest; the share of Mazuelo changes with the year.
wine.sites: La Plana, a single vineyard at the highest point of the Finca Ygay estate, at about 485 metres, south east of Logroño in Rioja Alta.
wine.making: Tempranillo and Mazuelo are aged apart for two to three years in 225 litre barrels, American oak for the Tempranillo and, in some years, French oak for the Mazuelo. Once blended the wine rests in concrete vats, then for years in bottle before the house releases it.
wine.glass: Ripe plum, black cherry and dried fig over tea leaf, cedar, wild Mediterranean herbs and dried flowers, with an iron, savoury edge; polished tannin, fresh acidity and a harmonious finish that lasts.
wine.ageing: Built to last for decades, and young even at thirty in a strong year, though it can be opened as soon as the house lets it go.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; with age it throws a sediment, so decant an older bottle with care; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The castle of the Ygay estate south east of Logroño: a bottling of the estate, not a separate property.
A Gran Reserva in law, aged five years at least; Especial is the house's own addition.
The title granted to the founder in 1872, and the name of the house.

records.table: Named for the castle of Marqués de Murrieta's Ygay estate by Logroño, Castillo Ygay is the house's Gran Reserva Especial, from La Plana and only in years it judges exceptional. Tempranillo with a little Mazuelo, savoury, with black cherry, fig and cedar, it rests long in barrel and bottle.
records.story: Luciano de Murrieta (1822 to 1911) was born in Peru and learnt the ways of Bordeaux before he turned to Rioja. In 1852, as the house tells it, he made his first Rioja with Bordeaux methods, in the Logroño cellars of the Duke of la Victoria, aiming for a wine that would endure over time. In 1872 the crown made him Marqués de Murrieta, and he set his house on the Ygay estate south east of the city, where the castle that names the flagship stands. Castillo Ygay became the estate's Gran Reserva Especial, reserved for vintages the house judged exceptional and held for years in barrel, then in bottle, before release. In 1983 the estate was bought by the Cebrián-Sagarriga family, who restored the castle, declared a museum in 2019, and later built a new winery beside it. The red is drawn from La Plana alone, and its white sister makes the house's point even more plainly: the Castillo Ygay Blanco of 1986 spent twenty one years in American oak. Castillo Ygay reads Rioja's five years for a Gran Reserva as a floor, not a target.

others.name: Castillo Ygay Blanco Gran Reserva Especial
others.note: Viura with Malvasía, held for decades in barrel and made in very rare years; the 1986 spent twenty one years in American oak.

others.name: Dalmau
others.note: The modern red of the house, Tempranillo with Cabernet Sauvignon and Graciano, aged in French oak.

others.name: Capellanía
others.note: A barrel aged white of Viura from a named parcel inside the Ygay estate.

traps: Castillo Ygay is a bottling of the Marqués de Murrieta estate, not a separate property.
Gran Reserva Especial is no legal rank: in law the wine is a Gran Reserva, and Especial is the house's own word.
Murrieta's Ygay estate lies south east of Logroño in Rioja Alta, not in Rioja Alavesa.

cards.front: Marqués de Murrieta: which vineyard gives Castillo Ygay?
cards.back: La Plana, the highest part of the Ygay estate, at about 485 metres, south east of Logroño.

cards.front: Which two grapes make Castillo Ygay, and how are they aged?
cards.back: Tempranillo, the great majority, and Mazuelo, aged apart in barrel for two to three years, then blended, rested in concrete and held in bottle.

questions.q: Castillo Ygay's label reads Gran Reserva Especial. How should a guest read the word Especial?
opts: In law it is a Gran Reserva; Especial is the house's word
Especial is a legal tier above Gran Reserva in Rioja
Especial marks a wine grown in Rioja Alavesa
Especial means it was aged in French oak alone
questions.exp: Rioja's ageing terms stop at Gran Reserva, at least five years with two in barrel and two in bottle; Especial is Murrieta's own word, not a higher legal tier.

questions.q: In 1852 Luciano de Murrieta made his first Rioja with methods learnt abroad. Where had he learnt them?
opts: In Bordeaux
In Jerez
In Porto
In Champagne
questions.exp: Murrieta brought the methods of Bordeaux to Rioja in 1852, seeking a red that would last; Jerez, Porto and Champagne make fortified and sparkling wines.

report: The purchase of Ygay is 1872 in one account, 1877 in another and the late 1870s in a third, and a house interview has the land bought in 1852; the story says the 1870s.

Luciano de Murrieta's dates and the title of 20 October 1872 rest on Wikipedia's list of the marquesses and the Kiddle mirror of the Spanish article; the Duke of la Victoria's cellars at Logroño on two secondary accounts.
The 1983 sale is in Wikipedia and Decanter; one other Decanter article says 1982. The castle museum of 2019 and the new winery of 2021 are the house's own news.

The making follows the house's pages for the 2010 and 2012 vintages (24 and 34 months in barrel, French oak for the Mazuelo in 2012, 20 months in concrete); La Plana's planting year is 1950 on one house page and 1940 on another, so it is left out.
Decanter's Wine Legend of the 1925 and the claim that Murrieta was the first Rioja house to export were left out for want of a second source.

The library's p-marques-de-murrieta and w-castillo-ygay call Castillo Ygay the region's longest held Gran Reserva, a rank no source searched confirms; the record does not say it, and the library is reported, not edited.
Searches for this record: 6 of the group's 35.

changed: story: "born in Arequipa in Peru"; now "born in Peru": Peru is in every account read, Arequipa only in Wikipedia and an interview on the house's site whose address names a living person, and one regional account differs on his parents, so the city is left out.

story: "in the 1870s he set his house on the Ygay estate"; now "he set his house on the Ygay estate", with no decade: the purchase is 1872 in one account, 1877 in another and 1852 in the house's own interview.

story: "who restored the castle, opened as a museum in 2019, and finished a new winery in 2021"; now "who restored the castle, declared a museum in 2019, and later built a new winery beside it": the house's museum statement has the restoration ended in 2015 and the castle declared a museum in 2019, and its own pages give 2021 and 2022 for the new winery.
open: The Logroño cellars of the Duke of la Victoria, where the first wine of 1852 was made, rest on the author's two secondary accounts; the house's pages searched here give 1852 and Bordeaux but not the cellars, and one regional account ties the property to the Duchess of la Victoria, Espartero's wife.

wine.name: Imperial Gran Reserva
wine.classification: Gran Reserva, an ageing category of the DOCa Rioja
wine.grapes: Tempranillo, the great majority, with Graciano and a little Mazuelo.
wine.sites: Small vineyards of Rioja Alta around Villalba and Torremontalbo, at about 550 to 650 metres.
wine.making: After the malolactic fermentation in concrete vats, the wine spends about two years in French and American oak barrels, racked every eight months, then at least three years in bottle in the house's century old cellars at Haro. Only exceptional years give it.
wine.glass: Deep cherry red; black cherry, bramble and liquorice over clove, roasted coffee, cigar leaf, chocolate and toffee, with a balsamic lift, velvety tannin and a long, fragrant finish.
wine.ageing: Ready on release after its years in barrel and bottle, it holds and deepens for many years in a cool cellar, turning towards leather, tobacco and dried fig.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, the house advising the upper end; an old bottle is decanted gently, its sediment left in the bottle; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Compañía Vinícola del Norte de España, the wine company of northern Spain; said Cune.
The brand, named from a special bottling for the English market in the imperial pint.
Rioja's legal ageing term above Reserva: five years at least, two in barrel and two in bottle.

records.table: Imperial Gran Reserva is CVNE's Rioja Alta red, from small vineyards near Haro and made in exceptional years alone: mostly Tempranillo with Graciano, two years in oak and three more in bottle. Expect dark cherry, clove and cigar leaf, and call the house Cune, as Spain does.
records.story: CVNE began in Haro in 1879, when two brothers of the Real de Asúa family set up a wine company near the town's railway station; the house traces the move to one brother's asthma, for which a doctor had prescribed a drier climate than that of Bilbao. Until 1882 the firm traded as Corcuera, Real de Asúa y Compañía, before it took the name Compañía Vinícola del Norte de España; its initials, read with the V as a U, gave the spoken name Cune. In 1909 the house raised a barrel hall whose steel roof spans it with no pillar inside, a design that a plaque in the hall credits to the engineer of the Eiffel Tower. Imperial followed in the 1920s, its name taken, in the house's telling, from a special bottling for the English market in the measure called the imperial pint. Viña Real, from the Rioja Alavesa side, gave the house a second voice, and descendants of the founding family kept control through the century. Imperial Gran Reserva is not made every year, only in exceptional ones, and it is aged in the old Haro cellars. Set beside Viña Real from Alavesa, it shows the Rioja Alta side of one house, and its label settles why CVNE is said Cune.

others.name: Viña Real Gran Reserva
others.note: The Rioja Alavesa counterpart, from the house's separate cellar above Laguardia: another subzone, not another tier.

others.name: Contino
others.note: A single estate at Laserna in Rioja Alavesa, part of the house and bottled under its own name.

others.name: Monopole
others.note: A white Rioja of Viura and one of the long standing white wine brands of Spain.

traps: Imperial is Rioja Alta and Viña Real is Rioja Alavesa: two subzones of one house, not two quality tiers.
Cune is how CVNE is spoken, from reading the V of its initials as a U; it is the same house.
Monopole is a brand of white Rioja, not a Burgundian monopole.

cards.front: CVNE: where does the name of its Imperial come from?
cards.back: A special bottling for the English market in the measure called the imperial pint, in the 1920s.

cards.front: Which subzone gives Imperial Gran Reserva, and which gives its sister Viña Real?
cards.back: Imperial is Rioja Alta, from vineyards near Haro; Viña Real is Rioja Alavesa, from a cellar above Laguardia.

questions.q: A guest compares CVNE's Imperial Gran Reserva with the Viña Real Gran Reserva of the same house. What separates the two?
opts: The subzone: Rioja Alta against Rioja Alavesa
The grape: Garnacha against Tempranillo
The legal tier: Gran Reserva against Crianza
The vessel: chestnut casks against steel
questions.exp: Imperial comes from Rioja Alta vineyards near Haro and Viña Real from Rioja Alavesa, each with its own cellar; both are led by Tempranillo and both are made as Gran Reservas.

questions.q: By CVNE's own account, its founders came to Haro in 1879 partly for one brother's health. From which city's damper climate had they come?
opts: Bilbao
Bordeaux
Madrid
Logroño
questions.exp: A doctor prescribed a drier climate than Bilbao's for one of the Real de Asúa brothers, as the house tells it; Logroño is Rioja's own capital, not the city they left.

report: The founders are described, not named with dates, for want of their dates; the asthma, the name Corcuera, Real de Asúa y Compañía until 1882 and the imperial pint are the house's own history.
Imperial is dated to the 1920s by the house's own pages and two secondary accounts (one gives 1920), while Decanter gives 1917 as the first vintage; the story says the 1920s.

The barrel hall of 1909 is credited to Gustave Eiffel by a plaque in the hall (Forbes) and called an attribution by another account, so the story says what the plaque says and names nobody; the Forbes page is not cited because its address names a living writer.
The house advises 18 degrees Celsius; the record gives 16 to 18, the Codex's reference for a full red, with the house's upper end.
The making follows the house's sheets for 2016 (over 24 months in barrel, racked every eight months, at least 36 months in bottle) and 2018 (new French and American oak).
The library's p-cvne calls Imperial and Viña Real the textbook Reserva and Gran Reserva (region record) and the cleanest way to examine the subzones: judgement words, reported and not edited.
Searches for this record: 4 of the group's 35, with the shared search of Haro's station quarter.

changed: questions[0].q: "with Viña Real from the same house"; now "with the Viña Real Gran Reserva of the same house": Viña Real is also bottled as a Crianza and a Reserva, so the tier option could be right for a guest holding one; naming the Gran Reserva leaves the subzone the one answer, as the explanation already says.
open: Imperial's first year: the house says the 1920s, while Decanter and a writer's piece republished on the house's site give a first vintage of 1917; the story keeps the house's 1920s.

The change of name in 1882 is read from the house's republished history, which gives Corcuera, Real de Asúa y Compañía as the full name until 1882; that the new name was taken that year is implied there rather than stated.

wine.name: Prado Enea Gran Reserva
wine.classification: Gran Reserva, an ageing category of the DOCa Rioja
wine.grapes: Tempranillo, the great majority, with Garnacha, Mazuelo and Graciano for the rest.
wine.sites: High vineyards of the house in the north west of Rioja Alta, around Sajazarra, Cellorigo and Fonzaleche, at 550 to 700 metres on calcareous clay and alluvial soils; always the last grapes Muga picks.
wine.making: Wood from vat to barrel: the wine ferments in the house's oak vats, then spends at least three years in barrels of American and French oak, racked by gravity and fined with egg white, and at least three more in bottle, leaving Haro six years and more after the vintage.
wine.glass: Bright black cherry in colour; ripe cherry and black plum over cedar, cocoa and warm sweet spice. A silky, juicy attack, medium body, lively acidity and very fine tannin; balsamic herbs linger at the end.
wine.ageing: Approachable when released, after six years and more, it keeps for many years beyond, its fruit drying as tobacco and leather come through.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant an older bottle with a steady hand and stop at the sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Muga picks Prado Enea's grapes last, from its coolest vineyards, and makes this Gran Reserva only when the year is exceptional: Tempranillo led, fermented in oak vats and kept six years and more in barrel and bottle before release. Beside roast lamb it pours silky, with cherry, cedar and cocoa.
records.story: A married couple founded Bodegas Muga in Haro in 1932, and the husband gave the house his surname. The house chose wood at every step: fermentation in oak vats, ageing in barrels its own coopers build and mend, racking by gravity and fining with egg white. At the end of the 1960s the family made the first Prado Enea, a Gran Reserva drawn from its coolest vineyards in the years it judged exceptional and in no others. In 1970 the family moved into a building of the Barrio de la Estación, Haro's station quarter, beside the houses founded there since 1877. The family later added Torre Muga, a modern red aged in French oak, so that the two styles of Rioja sit under one roof. Prado Enea's grapes are always the last the house picks, and the wine spends at least three years in barrel and three in bottle before it leaves Haro, a year past the law's five. Prado Enea is the traditional half of Muga's two styles: a Gran Reserva made in wood from vat to barrel, ready to drink when it leaves the cellar.

traps: Prado Enea is the traditional Gran Reserva and Torre Muga the modern French oak red: one house, two styles.
Haro, Muga's home, lies in Rioja Alta; do not place the house in Rioja Alavesa.
Prado Enea's six years in barrel and bottle pass the Gran Reserva rule of five; the extra year is the house's choice, not the law's.

cards.front: Bodegas Muga: which vineyards give Prado Enea, and when are they picked?
cards.back: High vineyards in the north west of Rioja Alta, at 550 to 700 metres; always the last grapes of the harvest.

cards.front: Prado Enea: what time in barrel and in bottle comes before its release?
cards.back: At least three years in American and French oak barrels and three more in bottle: six years and more in all.

questions.q: Bodegas Muga was founded in Haro in 1932. In which year did it move into the Barrio de la Estación?
questions.exp: The house was founded in 1932 and moved to the station quarter in 1970; 1879 is the founding of CVNE nearby, and 1913 the planting of López de Heredia's Tondonia.

report: The founders are described, not named with dates: their dates were found nowhere, and the founder's grandson, who shares his name, is living.
Decanter derives the name Prado Enea from a building once owned by Dionisio del Prado, known locally as the house of Prado; no second source was found, so the story does not say it.

The first Prado Enea is 1969 in Decanter and 1968 in one other account, so the story says the end of the 1960s; the founder's death in the 1960s and the passing of the house to three children rest on one account and are left out.

The house's own Gran Reserva page gives three years in barrel and three in bottle, and one house tasting page says twelve months in oak barrels, likely the time in large vats before the barrels; the record follows the three and three.

The house's page says the Barrio building is two hundred years old; no second source confirms it, so the story says a building of the quarter. The 1970 move rests on Spanish Wine Lover and a second account.
Fermentation with no added yeast and no temperature control in vats of 10,000 kilos rests on one account and is left out; the oak vats themselves are the library's.
Searches for this record: 8 of the group's 35.

wine.making: "Fermented in large oak vats, as every Muga red is ... racked by hand"; now "Fermented in the house's oak vats ... racked by gravity": the house's pages say racking by gravity, and they give wooden vats rather than oak for some other reds, so every red is not said.
